extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of logic and philosophy (undergraduate/graduate level)
extracted.subtask_description: Explication of what propositions assert, the difference between verbal and real propositions, the five kinds of matters of fact (existence, co-existence, sequence, causation, resemblance), and the logical doctrine of classification and predicables (genus, species, differentia, proprium, accidens).

rubrics_metrics.name: Five kinds of matters-of-fact asserted in non‑verbal propositions
rubrics_metrics.description: Every proposition (that is not merely verbal) affirms (or denies) one of five kinds of matters-of-fact: Existence, Co-existence (Order in Place), Sequence (Order in Time), Causation, or Resemblance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This five-fold division is presented as exhaustive for all things that can be believed or asserted; any non-verbal proposition can be classified under one of these five species and analyzed accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction within Co-existence: Order in Place vs Co‑inherence of attributes
rubrics_metrics.description: Propositions of co-existence come in two kinds: (a) those taking account of Place (Order in Place), and (b) co-inherence of attributes (concurrence of two or more attributes in the same part or locality), as exemplified by physical substances or mental faculties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that co-inherence (attributes concurring in the same part/locality) is conceptually distinct from order in place; co-inherence often pertains to simultaneity and belongs to Time rather than Place. Use examples (gold: weight, hardness, color; mind: feeling, will, thought) to decide which variety is asserted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Class‑names (connotative general names) may predicate mere resemblance
rubrics_metrics.description: When the predicate is the name of a class founded on unanalyzable resemblance (e.g., sensations like 'white'), the proposition often asserts only resemblance: that the subject is like other things previously called by that name.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat predicates that denote classes of simple sensations as conveying likeness to past experiences rather than analysable attributes; the connotation is a mere resemblance and the proposition communicates that similarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstract terms can be rendered into equivalent concrete propositions
rubrics_metrics.description: An abstract name denotes an attribute (or combination of attributes) and any proposition with abstract terms can be transformed into an equivalent proposition using concrete terms (either the concrete things that connote the attribute or the 'fundamenta'—the facts/phenomena grounding the attribute).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To clarify meaning and factual content, translate abstract propositions into concrete ones (e.g., 'Thoughtlessness is dangerous' → 'Thoughtless actions are dangerous') and then analyze which of the five kinds of matter-of-fact is being asserted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Merely verbal propositions (about the meaning of names)
rubrics_metrics.description: Propositions that relate only to the signification of names are not strictly true or false but conform or do not conform to usage or convention; their only possible proof is proof of linguistic usage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify propositions that assert nothing beyond the conventional meaning of words; such propositions do not bear on factual matters and are assessed by checking usage/definition rather than empirical truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Essential versus accidental (non‑essential) propositions
rubrics_metrics.description: Essential propositions predicate attributes that are already connoted by the subject-name (thus largely verbal and conveying no new information), while accidental (non-essential) propositions predicate attributes not connoted by the name and therefore convey real information about things.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat 'essential' claims as analytically true from the meaning of the term (useful mainly as definitions), whereas 'accidental' claims are substantive and informative. Note the linguistic ambiguity of the copula can make essential propositions seem to imply existence; actual informative content often comes from assuming real existence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two modes of expressing general propositions: theoretical vs practical
rubrics_metrics.description: A general proposition can be expressed theoretically (e.g., 'the attributes of A are always accompanied by attribute B') or practically as a memorandum (e.g., 'the attributes of A are a mark or evidence of B').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For reasoning and application, prefer the practical mode (propositions as marks/evidence) since it better indicates how propositions function to lead us from known to unknown cases; both modes are equivalent but emphasize different uses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role and form of Definitions (as useful essential propositions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Definitions are the most useful kind of essential propositions; to be complete a definition should unfold the entire connotation of the name (though commonly only enough attributes are specified to distinguish the intended objects).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When drafting or evaluating a definition, aim to capture the connotation comprehensively if the purpose requires full precision; otherwise, include sufficient attributes to mark the class against other known objects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Doctrine of the Predicables: genus, species, differentia, proprium, accidens
rubrics_metrics.description: General names (when predicated) fall under five predicables: genus, species, differentia, proprium, and accidens. These categories do not denote fixed meanings of the names themselves but the relation the predicate bears to the subject in the particular predication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify predicates by their relation to the subject in each instance (e.g., 'animal' is genus relative to man but species relative to Being). Do not treat names as intrinsically belonging to a single predicable; their role depends on context and the level of classification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification arises from attributes connoted by general names
rubrics_metrics.description: By introducing a general (connotative) name we create a class composed of things that possess the connoted attributes; sometimes names are introduced primarily to form classes for convenience (taxonomic purposes), but their signification remains constituted by attributes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In constructing or evaluating classifications, ground groupings in explicit attributes (connotations). Recognize that names invented for classificatory convenience still denote attributes and should be treated like other connotative names; the principles regulating 'good' classification are to be applied (they are to be treated in more detail elsewhere).
